lesson: Vomiting and deep breathing — a DKA reasoning case
voice_profile: Use the established MeducateMe Chatterbox voice reference. The delivery should sound like Dr Volker Krause teaching one learner at the bedside: calm, warm, intelligent and conversational. Use short sentences, occasional pauses and questions. Do not sound like an announcer and do not simply read the words on screen. Explain why each clue matters and let the learner think before the answer is given.

stages.script: Okay, have a look at this child first. Twelve years old. Three days of being very thirsty and passing urine all the time. Since yesterday, vomiting, some abdominal discomfort, and getting increasingly lethargic. And now today the breathing has become really deep and rapid. The heart rate is up, the child looks dehydrated, but the oxygen saturation is ninety-nine percent. So before you jump to a diagnosis, ask yourself: what here does not fit simple gastroenteritis? The vomiting could fit. The lethargy could fit. But that breathing pattern should make you stop. Why is this child breathing like that? Pick your answer, then we will build it from there.

Right. Now do not name the disease yet. Just put the clues together. Thirst. Polyuria. Dehydration. Then vomiting. And on top of that, deep rapid breathing. The normal oxygen saturation is useful because it makes a primary oxygenation problem less convincing. So the lungs may actually be responding to something happening elsewhere. Think metabolically. What could give you lots of urine, volume loss, and then a respiratory response like this? Keep that thought in your head. Now let us look at the bloods.

Now the picture becomes much clearer. Glucose is twenty-eight. Ketones are five point six. The pH is seven point one two, and the bicarbonate is eight. So this child has a significant metabolic acidosis. The carbon dioxide is low because the child is blowing off carbon dioxide to compensate. That explains the deep breathing. Now look at the potassium: four point eight. It looks reassuring, but it is not. In DKA the total body potassium is usually depleted, even when the serum potassium is normal or high, because potassium has shifted out of cells while a lot has also been lost in the urine. Before you reveal the diagnosis, identify the acid-base disturbance on the screen.

So yes, this is diabetic ketoacidosis. But I do not want you to just recognise DKA. I want you to see why it happens. Start with the missing signal: insulin. Without enough insulin, the liver keeps putting glucose into the blood, while muscle and fat do not handle glucose normally. The glucose rises. Once there is enough glucose in the filtrate, the kidney cannot reabsorb all of it, so glucose stays in the urine and pulls water with it. That gives you osmotic diuresis, dehydration and thirst. At the same time, insulin is no longer suppressing lipolysis. Fat is broken down, free fatty acids go to the liver, and the liver turns them into ketones. Those ketones are acids. So one missing hormone gives you two linked problems: severe water loss from hyperglycaemia, and metabolic acidosis from ketones.

Now go back to the child and explain every finding. The polyuria comes from glycosuria and osmotic diuresis. The thirst is the body's response to losing all that water. The tachycardia comes from the falling circulating volume. The vomiting and abdominal pain are common when ketosis, acidosis and dehydration become significant. And the deep breathing now makes complete sense. The pH is low, so the respiratory system tries to compensate by getting rid of carbon dioxide. That is Kussmaul breathing. It is not primarily a lung problem. It is the lungs trying to rescue the acid-base balance. Once you can derive the signs like this, you do not have to memorise them as a disconnected list.

Treatment is basically the physiology in reverse. First, fluid restores the circulation and begins correcting the water deficit. Insulin is crucial, not just because it brings the glucose down, but because it switches off lipolysis and stops further ketone production. Then there is potassium. Remember, the total body potassium is depleted. Once you give insulin, potassium moves back into cells, so the serum level can fall quite quickly. That is why potassium has to be watched and replaced appropriately. Also remember that the glucose often improves before the ketoacidosis is fully corrected. If that happens, you add dextrose so that you can keep the insulin running safely until ketogenesis has stopped. And throughout all of this, keep checking the neurological state because cerebral injury is the complication we are most worried about.

Okay, one last time. Rebuild the whole case from the beginning. Insulin falls. Glucose rises and lipolysis switches on. The high glucose spills into the urine, water follows it, and the child becomes polyuric, thirsty and dehydrated. Meanwhile the liver converts fatty acids into ketones. The ketones cause metabolic acidosis. Bicarbonate falls. The lungs compensate by blowing off carbon dioxide, which gives you the deep rapid breathing. That single chain explains the history, the examination and the blood results. And treatment simply attacks each part of that physiology. If you can reconstruct that story without memorising a list, then you properly understand this case.
